items.title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
items.summary: US regulators have approved SpaceX's Starmind project, which aims to deploy up to one million satellites to function as orbital data centres for AI computing. The initiative seeks to bypass terrestrial power and cooling constraints, though it faces criticism regarding space congestion and light pollution.

brief.what: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has granted SpaceX approval to launch a constellation of one million satellites designed to process AI data in orbit. The project, Starmind, will utilize solar power to manage computing loads that exceed current terrestrial capabilities, with deployment milestones set for 2035 and 2038.
brief.who: SpaceX, led by Elon Musk, is the project developer, while the FCC serves as the regulatory body. Amazon, the American Astronomical Society, and Earthjustice are primary critics of the plan.
brief.context: Traditional data centres face increasing opposition on Earth due to their high energy and water consumption. SpaceX proposes orbital centres as a greener, more efficient alternative to meet the surging demand for AI computing power.
brief.why: The FCC claims the project supports America's super intelligence economy and technological leadership. Conversely, critics like Amazon label it a lofty ambition, while astronomers warn that the large, bright satellites will significantly interfere with night sky observations and increase space debris risks.
brief.next: SpaceX intends to launch the first Starmind satellite next year, though technical experts note that the necessary high-capacity laser communication links have not yet been fully perfected.

brief.why: The transition occurs as Christine Lagarde concludes her term early, necessitating a new leader to direct the bank's ongoing fight against inflation and potential bond turmoil.

items.title: Nigeria Boosts Retail Supply of Dollars to Curb Naira Volatility
items.author: Emele Onu and Nduka Orjinmo
items.summary: The Central Bank of Nigeria is increasing the supply of dollars available to retail customers to stabilize the naira. This move aims to improve local liquidity and mitigate recent currency volatility.

brief.what: The Central Bank of Nigeria has authorized a significant increase in the sale of US dollars to retail customers. This intervention is intended to address the recent depreciation of the naira and improve liquidity within the local market.
brief.who: The Central Bank of Nigeria is the primary actor, acting as the regulatory authority managing the nation's monetary policy and currency stability.
brief.context: The naira has experienced downward pressure and lost value throughout the current month, prompting the central bank to intervene in the retail foreign exchange market.
brief.why: The bank initiated this policy to boost local liquidity and ease the ongoing pressure on the naira, which has been volatile recently.

items.title: Orangutans face bleak future after Indonesia’s devastating wildfires
items.author: Dyna Rochmyaningsih
items.summary: Severe wildfires in Indonesia have destroyed 60% of Bornean orangutan habitats in Kalimantan, exacerbated by a super El Niño climate event. Researchers report that toxic air quality and widespread forest loss are displacing orangutans and threatening their survival.

brief.what: Indonesia is facing one of its most severe fire and haze seasons in three decades, with over 2.8 million hectares burned. The fires have destroyed 60% of Bornean orangutan habitats in Kalimantan, leading to significant displacement and resource competition among the critically endangered species.
brief.who: Primates researcher Erin Vogel and her research team at the Tuanan Orangutan Research Station are documenting the impact of the fires on the Bornean orangutan population.
brief.context: The region experienced roughly 300,000 blazes between July and October, with air quality reaching toxic levels 400 times higher than World Health Organization safety standards.
brief.why: The disaster is attributed to a super El Niño event that dried out vegetation and generated winds that fueled the flames, creating a severe climate and health crisis.

items.title: COP31 ends with no deal after negotiators fail to reach an agreement on fossil fuels
items.author: Rachel Waldholz
items.summary: International climate negotiations at COP31 concluded without a formal agreement after delegates failed to reach a consensus on fossil fuel policy. The breakdown was driven by disagreements over transitioning away from coal, oil, and gas, alongside disputes regarding climate funding for developing nations.

also.author: Jacqueline Peel, Professor of Law, The University of Melbourne
also.title: How did the COP31 climate agreement fall apart – and what happens now?
also.note: The Conversation frames the story by focusing on the mechanics of the collapse and the future implications of the failed agreement.

brief.what: The COP31 climate summit in Turkey ended without a deal after nearly 200 nations failed to agree on a framework for addressing climate change. Negotiations stalled primarily over the inclusion of language regarding a global transition away from fossil fuels and the provision of financial support for developing countries.
brief.who: Key actors included the European Union and small island states, which pushed for fossil fuel phase-outs, and oil-producing nations like Saudi Arabia, which blocked such language. Ireland’s environment minister Darragh O'Brien and Marshall Islands representative Kathy Jetnil-Kijiner criticized the lack of progress, while the U.S. was absent due to its withdrawal from negotiations.
brief.context: The annual climate summit has been held since 1995 to address global warming. Developing nations argue that wealthy countries, which are historically responsible for climate change, have failed to meet funding promises established under the Paris Climate Agreement.
brief.why: Talks collapsed because the European Union determined that no deal was preferable to one that failed to explicitly address fossil fuels. Additionally, developing nations expressed frustration over insufficient financial support for climate-related disasters.

items.title: The leading cities in the world for high-quality research in 2025
items.author: Bec Crew
items.summary: Beijing maintains its top position in the Nature Index for natural sciences research, while Chinese cities increasingly dominate global rankings in chemistry and environmental sciences. Conversely, several US cities have seen their research output rankings decline over the past decade.

brief.what: Beijing continues to lead global research output in the natural sciences, with Chinese cities occupying all top ten spots in chemistry rankings. Between 2016 and 2025, Beijing and Shanghai achieved significant growth in chemistry, each increasing their adjusted Share by nearly 900 points.
brief.who: The Nature Index tracks research output, with the report supported by the Beijing Municipal Science & Technology Commission and the Administrative Commission of Zhongguancun Science Park.
brief.context: The Nature Index measures high-quality research output through a metric called 'Share,' which tracks contributions to research articles published in selected journals. This data highlights a shifting geographical landscape in scientific research, marked by the rise of Chinese urban centers and the decline of some previously prominent US cities.
brief.why: The article attributes these shifts to the evolving research output and adjusted Share metrics of cities globally, noting that Beijing contributed 25% of China’s Earth and environmental sciences Share in 2025.
